interactions.title: The gods watch Dunmar
lines: DM: Bhishma, the mother of Dunmar, demigoddess and soul of the people of the plains, the keeper of memories and stories. Her attention is focused on a small camp in the northern part of her country, where much of what is left of her power on Taelgar gathers. The open wound of her ruined home distracts her, as always, but she watches anyway, hoping perhaps that something will change.

DM: Shakun, her daughter, demigoddess of magic and illusion and the defender of Dunmar, weaver of mazes to confound the enemies of her people, feels her mother's absence as she still works to mend the web of energy that binds and powers her protections. Much is lost now and must be repaired, and she is still weakened by ordeals.

DM: Laka, her father, god of knowledge and time, the ancestors, and the seasons, the cycles of history, watches the servants travel back towards Tokra, hoping they have learned what they needed from their journey.

DM: Aagir, god of battle, fire, and death, protector of those who fight, defender of the honor of his people, gazes east, as always, his warnings and call to action still unheeded, still looking for a champion to take them up. But as he watches the fire in the heart of the one just returned to him grow, he wonders.

DM: Sonkar, goddess of justice and truth, of purity and beauty and artisans, the judge of the souls of the dead, watches all her people, seeing the souls of those who died struggle to find her, worried, as always, about war, about the lost lives of those who may soon die out of time, about the beauty they will no longer create, seeing more clearly than any of her siblings the futures cut short.

DM: Jeevali, goddess of home and hearth, family, life and rebirth, the eldest of the siblings and the peacemaker among sometimes fractious relationships among her siblings, is focused, as ever she is at this time of year, on the rain, on pushing the water-laden clouds as far east as she can, keeping the lifeblood of her people alive.

DM: Chidya, goddess of the wild, of horses, nature, a free spirit, a symbol of love, watches over all those who travel, outcasts and the lost, the refugees and those who wander because they must, watching them find their place to return, some joy coming to her, though the memory of all that was lost in the great war still haunts her at times, seeing her people scattered across the plains.

lines: Kenzo: Before we go to bed, though I do my interview with the keeper.

Kenzo: What made you start the—

DM: Oh wow, that's quite interesting. Before, before I started the inn, I was a young lad, rode off with Shandan warband. He was recruiting some you know, young folks to come protect the trade going to Songara. There'd been lots of these little dragon like creatures, kobolds they're called. And raiding, horse thieving, things like that, so I joined up. There was a good five years. Plenty of, plenty of action.

DM: Rode mostly along the Myraeni Gap near Songara. Killing some of these little bastards stealing our stuff, until I was wounded. Cut my leg up pretty bad, broke real bad, couldn't, couldn't really fight after that.
DM: They are vicious little creatures. Think you've got them cornered, then they'll run off, lead you straight into some death trap. Horrible little little bastard got me.
DM: Anyway. Came back here, didn't quite know what to do, but with a big sack of gold so I started an inn.

DM: Not stayed at my inn. There's been a few that have passed through. Occasionally they'll come stay in the monastery. Not for the past seven years, eight years.
DM: Now what's—these past few months have gotta be some of the craziest in my time in Tokra. It's normally pretty quiet town, to be honest.
DM: Get some Chardonians coming in. They tip well. Usually.
Kenzo: There's blood on the money, though, when they give it to you right usually?
DM: Yeah, I mean, it's money, right.
DM: Where did you get your money from? I mean, this inn is founded on blood money, if you want to be honest about it. Kobold blood, but you know blood nonetheless.
Kenzo: Ain't that the truth. And what about your family? What about—you have any, do you have a partner, any children?
DM: Never found the right person. Parents still live here, they're quite old now, and Dad died a couple years ago, but keep my mom, you know, take care of her.
DM: Had my wild time and my youth. Now I just want to—things are good, keep them good. Don't rock the boat.

Kenzo: And what would you say, maybe to wrap up what's—if you were to tell your story, what would you think you'd want to share to the world so that they would remember you by? What would you want the—how would you want to be remembered?
DM: I built this place. I don't know who I'll leave it to. Still got some years in me left. Maybe I'll find somebody so.
